ASGE Guideline on the Role of Endoscopy in Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding
  • Source: Gastrointestinal Endoscopy, Vol. ■, No. ■: 2026
  • Topic: Role of endoscopy in acute lower GI bleeding (LGIB)
  • Author(s): Forbes N, Coelho-Prabhu N, et al. (ASGE Standards of Practice Committee)
Definition and Epidemiology
  • LGIB --> bleeding from cecum, colon, or rectum
  • Typically presents as hematochezia (less commonly melena)
  • Annual hospitalization rates: 20–40 per 100,000 persons in US and Europe
  • Rates higher in patients with comorbidities and those on antithrombotic medications
Etiology Distribution
  • Diverticular disease: ~30% of LGIB presentations (most common)
  • Anorectal pathology: ~20%
  • Colonic neoplasms: ~20%
  • Various colitides: ~20%
  • Less common --> iatrogenic (post-endoscopic/surgical), vascular lesions (angioectasia)
Mortality and Risk Factors
  • Mortality: 2%–4%
  • Higher risk --> advanced age, coagulopathy, concomitant comorbidities
Initial Assessment
Evaluation and Risk Stratification
  • Full medical history and physical examination required
  • Key factors to assess:
  • Advanced age
  • Relevant comorbidities
  • Baseline medications (especially antithrombotic agents)
  • Initial hemodynamic stability
  • Ongoing bleeding status
  • Risk scores exist for stratification (e.g., Oakland score, SHA₂PE score)
  • Risk scores --> identify patients safe for discharge/outpatient investigation
  • Clinical judgment should supersede risk score calculations
Resuscitation
  • Hemodynamically unstable patients --> observe in monitored setting
  • IV crystalloid fluids to normalize heart rate and blood pressure
  • Place 2 large-bore IV catheters (or equivalent)
  • Transfusion strategy:
  • Restrictive approach for most patients without cardiovascular disease history
  • Threshold: Hemoglobin <7 g/dL
  • Liberal strategy may be appropriate for patients with cardiovascular disease or acute coronary syndrome
Exclusion of Proximal Bleeding Source
  • Recommendation: Upper endoscopy should be performed for all patients with hematochezia and initial hemodynamic instability to rule out upper GI source (unless direct imaging evidence of LGIB exists)
  • RCT of 85 patients with suspected LGIB and hemodynamic instability:
  • Upper GI source identified in 15% of patients
  • Most common etiologies: peptic ulcers, esophagogastric varices
  • Subsequent upper endoscopy yield (when initial colonoscopy negative): 11%–22%
  • Risk factors for UGIB in patients with hematochezia:
  • Male sex
  • History of peptic ulcer disease or cirrhosis
  • BUN-to-creatinine ratio >30
  • Alternative for stable patients: urgent/emergent capsule endoscopy
Diagnostic Tests
Colonoscopy vs CT +/- Angiography
  • Recommendation: Either CT with contrast +/- angiography OR colonoscopy is acceptable as initial diagnostic modality
  • ASGE suggests: Colonoscopy for stable patients or after initial resuscitation
  • ASGE suggests: CT +/- angiography for ongoing hemodynamic instability
  • (Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence)
Meta-Analysis Findings (8 retrospective cohort studies)
Outcome CT +/- Angiography vs Colonoscopy
30-day mortality ↑ OR 12.64 (95% CI: 2.97–53.75)
Blood transfusion requirement ↑ OR 2.29 (95% CI: 1.56–3.35)
Hospital length of stay ↑ SMD 2.09 days (95% CI: 0.62–3.56)
Diagnostic yield No difference (OR 1.44; CI: 0.74–2.82)
Initial hemostasis ability No difference (OR 0.77; CI: 0.25–2.42)
  • CT patients were older, had more comorbidities, lower blood pressures, more transfusions
  • Likely reflects selection bias (most severe cases → CT)
  • Hemostasis rates with radiologic intervention: 19%–29%
  • Severe confounding limits comparison reliability
Clinical Decision Algorithm
  • Stable patients --> colonoscopy recommended
  • Unstable patients who respond to resuscitation --> colonoscopy acceptable
  • Ongoing hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation --> CT +/- angiography (followed by radiologic intervention if positive)
  • Expectant management appropriate for stable patients without transfusion requirement, especially with recent high-quality colonoscopy
Nuclear Medicine Modalities
  • Role now largely limited to settings where CT or endoscopy unavailable or inconclusive
  • Availability and performance of CT have reduced need for nuclear medicine in LGIB
Timing of Colonoscopy
Urgent vs Nonurgent Colonoscopy
  • Recommendation: Colonoscopy should be performed when patient is stable enough for procedure and able to tolerate full bowel preparation, regardless of timing
  • (Conditional recommendation, moderate quality evidence)
Meta-Analysis Findings (18 studies; 4 RCTs)
Outcome Urgent (<24h) vs Nonurgent Colonoscopy
30-day mortality No difference (OR 0.76; CI: 0.16–3.50)
Recurrent bleeding No difference overall (OR 1.23; CI: 0.46–3.27)
Recurrent bleeding (sensitivity analysis, 24h cutoff only) ↑ with urgent colonoscopy (OR 3.05; CI: 1.23–7.56)
Hospital length of stay Shorter with urgent colonoscopy (SMD –0.96 days; CI: –1.46 to –0.47)
Need for surgery No difference (OR 0.83; CI: 0.20–3.54)
Need for radiologic intervention No difference (OR 4.91; CI: 0.81–29.80)
Transfusion requirements No difference (OR 1.27; CI: 0.66–2.44)
Adverse events No difference (OR 1.39; CI: 0.45–4.35)
Clinical Considerations
  • If colonoscopy pursued within 24 hours:
  • Full bowel preparation required
  • Perform in controlled setting with multiple devices/techniques available
  • Earlier colonoscopy may reduce length of stay but implementation limited by:
  • Access to endoscopy
  • After-hours staffing issues (especially in nonacademic settings)
  • Exceptions allowing more urgent/unprepped colonoscopy:
  • Known/strongly suspected distal bleeding source
  • Iatrogenic bleeding at known identifiable location (postpolypectomy, post-EMR, post-endoscopic submucosal dissection)
Colonoscopy Preparation
Prepped vs Unprepped Colonoscopy
  • Recommendation: ASGE recommends colonoscopy with full bowel preparation unless strong suspicion of distal bleeding source or iatrogenic bleeding with known location
  • (Strong recommendation, very low quality evidence)
Evidence
  • Retrospective cohort study of 194 patients:
  • Full PEG-based bowel preparation vs enemas for hematochezia
  • Full prep --> higher diagnostic yield, ability to provide initial hemostasis, decreased need for repeat colonoscopy
Exceptions (see Figure 1)
  • Strongly suspected distal source of bleeding
  • Iatrogenic source at known, easily identifiable location:
  • Postpolypectomy
  • Post-EMR
  • Post-endoscopic submucosal dissection
  • Suspected rectal tube trauma/ulceration
Special Consideration: Radiation Proctopathy
  • Distal source but still requires full bowel preparation before APC
  • Reason: risk of colonic explosion with APC use and higher intestinal gas levels
Endoscopic Interventions for Diverticular Bleeding
Band Ligation vs Clipping
  • Recommendation: For active/recent diverticular bleeding, ASGE suggests band ligation OR clipping based on:
  • Location of bleeding
  • Clinical expertise
  • Device availability
  • For transverse colon or more proximal lesions: ASGE suggests band ligation when feasible
  • For distal lesions: ASGE suggests clipping
  • (Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence)
Meta-Analysis Findings (7 comparative studies; all observational)
Outcome Band Ligation vs Clipping
Recurrent bleeding ↓ with banding (OR 0.33; CI: 0.23–0.47)
Recurrent bleeding (right-sided lesions only) ↓ with banding
Recurrent bleeding (left-sided lesions) No apparent benefit of banding
Need for radiologic intervention ↓ with banding (OR 0.43; CI: 0.24–0.76)
Transfusion requirements Trend ↓ with banding (OR 0.73; CI: 0.52–1.02)
Need for surgery No difference (OR 1.08; CI: 0.36–3.23)
Adverse events Trend ↑ with banding (OR 2.41; CI: 0.70–8.24)
Adverse Events Observed
  • Band ligation: perforation (required surgery 100% of time), diverticulitis, fever
  • Clipping: diverticulitis
Technical Considerations for Banding
  • Most studies used band ligators on gastroscopes
  • Colonoscope-specific devices limited but available
  • Requires removal of scope to load device, then reinsertion
  • Can be technically challenging in angulated/redundant colon with active bleeding
  • Reidentification of bleeding site can be aided by:
  • Initial placement of marking clip
  • Tattoo (permanent, helps guide future management)
  • Banding should only be attempted by experienced providers with appropriate device available
Direct vs Indirect Clipping
  • Recommendation: When clipping is chosen for diverticular bleeding, ASGE suggests direct clipping over indirect clipping whenever feasible, particularly in proximal colon
  • (Conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence)
Techniques Defined
  • Indirect clipping: Closes entire diverticular orifice (may require "zipper" closure with multiple clips)
  • Direct clipping: Directly visualizes vessel (within diverticulum dome or along lip) and applies clips directly to vessel
Meta-Analysis Findings (9 comparative studies; all observational)
Outcome Direct vs Indirect Clipping
Initial hemostasis No difference (OR 1.17; CI: 0.43–3.20)
Mortality No difference (OR 3.39; CI: 0.27–42.21)
Recurrent bleeding ↓ with direct clipping (OR 0.58; CI: 0.44–0.77)
Need for radiologic intervention ↓ with direct clipping (OR 0.50; CI: 0.25–0.97)
Need for surgery No difference (OR 1.03; CI: 0.12–8.68)
Adverse events No difference (OR 1.27; CI: 0.25–6.46)
Transfusion requirements No difference (OR 0.88; CI: 0.42–1.82)
Situations Where Direct Clipping May Not Be Feasible
  • Small-mouthed diverticula
  • Lack of visibility of clear vessel/bleeding source to target
Endoscopic Management by Bleeding Type
Diverticular Bleeding
  • Band ligation or clipping recommended based on:
  • Location (right-sided → band ligation if feasible; left-sided → clipping)
  • Clinical expertise
  • Device availability
  • When clipping used --> direct over indirect when feasible
Other Modalities Considered
  • Snare ligation: Limited study but studied for diverticular bleeding
  • Over-the-scope clipping (OTSC): Early evidence promising but not extensively studied for acute diverticular bleeding
  • Thermal modalities: Caution required due to thin-walled anatomy and perforation risk
  • Risk minimized if applied at rim (not base) of diverticula
  • Use lower power and shorter duration
  • Topical hemostatic agents: Limited evidence (including self-assembling peptide gels)
  • Doppler probes: Data lacking for LGIB; further research warranted
Postresection Bleeding
  • Recommendation: Through-the-scope clipping or thermal coagulation as initial modalities; hemostatic powder for adjunctive use or refractory bleeding
Characteristics
  • Delayed bleeding after polypectomy, EMR, endoscopic submucosal dissection
  • Typically presents within 14 days (rarely up to 30 days)
  • Predictors of active bleeding at colonoscopy:
  • Left-sided lesions
  • Pedunculated lesions
  • Anticoagulant use
Management Options
  • Through-the-scope clip application: Proven effective
  • Contact thermal therapy: Must apply cautiously to resection bed (perforation risk, especially right colon)
  • Noncontact thermal therapy: Same caution applies
  • Epinephrine injection: Temporizing measure only
  • Hemostatic powder: Successful as monotherapy, combination therapy, or rescue therapy
Decision Analysis
  • Repeat colonoscopy for suspected delayed postpolypectomy bleeding beneficial in 22% of cases to identify/treat bleeding lesion
  • Number needed to treat: 4.5 patients
Bleeding Vascular Lesions (Angioectasia, Radiation Proctopathy)
  • Recommendation: Argon plasma coagulation (APC) recommended
Characteristics
  • Most often present with occult blood loss and anemia
  • Acute overt LGIB also possible
  • Risk factors for active bleeding:
  • Advanced patient age
  • Cardiac comorbidities
  • Anticoagulant use
  • Multiple lesions
  • Small lesions
APC Technique Considerations
  • Pulsed APC modes: More superficial cauterization than continuous modes
  • For right colon (thinner wall): Consider submucosal injection before APC to mitigate perforation risk
  • Recurrent bleeding rate after APC therapy: 7.4%
Alternative Technique (case series)
  • Submucosal injection → EMR-like resection → submucosal coagulation of exposed feeding vessel
  • Demonstrated successful eradication
Radiation Proctopathy
  • Considered a vascular lesion causing significant hematochezia
  • APC successfully treats bleeding in this population
Malignant Bleeding
  • Recommendation: Hemostatic powder or Nd:YAG laser for temporary hemostasis (palliative intent or bridge to definitive surgical management)
Key Points
  • Endoscopic therapy viewed as temporizing only
  • Nd:YAG laser described but limited evidence; waning availability in Western settings
  • Hemostatic powder: Demonstrates promise for immediate temporary hemostasis (more widely available now)
Role of Surgery
Indications
  • Recommendation: Surgery should be considered a last resort for acute LGIB, performed only when:
  • Bleeding not amenable to endoscopic or radiologic intervention
  • Both endoscopic and radiologic interventions have failed
Historical Context
  • Role of surgery much more limited with advancement of endoscopic and radiologic technologies
  • Surgery rates decreased from 22.6% (1988–1997) to 16.6% (1998–2006) in one cohort study of 1112 patients
  • Most recent data: Only 0.2% required surgery in UK nationwide audit of 2528 patients
Comparative Outcomes
  • Surgery vs interventional radiology (after positive CT angiography):
  • Surgical patients: younger, higher base excess and lactate levels
  • Hospital length of stay: similar between groups
  • Adverse event rates: higher with surgery
Emergency Surgery Outcomes (1614 patients)
  • 30-day mortality: 12.2%
  • Factors increasing short-term mortality:
  • Older age
  • Functional dependence
  • Higher American Society of Anesthesiologists score
  • Factors decreasing mortality:
  • Laparoscopic approach
  • Higher hematocrit at time of surgery
Exceptional Cases Requiring Emergent Laparotomy
  • Aortocolonic fistula
  • Bleeding Meckel's diverticulum
Sustainability Perspective
ASGE Recommendations for Sustainable Practice

1. Avoid low-yield procedures and duplicative testing (e.g., forego CT in stable LGIB; involve gastroenterology early)

2. Reduce hospital admissions, unnecessary procedures, and length of stay for low-risk patients using risk prediction tools

3. Aim to perform definitive endoscopic therapy at index procedure to avoid repeat procedures, prolonged hospitalizations, and readmissions

Future Research Directions
  • More RCTs to assess differences in approaches/techniques (minimize confounding)
  • Comparative studies adequately powered for adverse events with novel techniques
  • Studies assessing learning curves for novel techniques
  • Cost-effectiveness studies to understand impacts of various approaches/techniques
  • Studies on currently understudied interventions:
  • Over-the-scope clipping (OTSC)
  • Band ligation therapy
  • Doppler probe-directed therapy
  • Capsule endoscopy utility and indications in LGIB
Figures
Figure 1: Clinical decision-making algorithm for patients presenting with acute lower GI bleeding. *Examples might include patients with stable bleeding and a recent high-quality colonoscopy showing only diverticulosis. **The timing of endoscopic evaluation for nonsevere lower GI bleeding has not been associated with improved outcomes. ***Examples might include postpolypectomy/endoscopic submucosal dissection/EMR bleeding, malignancy with known location, known left-sided diverticular disease, and rectal trauma. ****If unavailable or unsuccessful and ongoing severe bleeding, consider urgent colonoscopy with expedited purgative bowel preparation or surgery.
